title: Sariputra transformed
hook: the goddess switches bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed

segments.voice: Yesterday, heavenly flowers slid off the bodhisattvas and clung to the disciples who called them improper. Your line: the flowers stick. Was it the thing, or your grip on it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

Shariputra is still sitting there with petals on his robe, and he has a question for the goddess. She's clearly wise. She's just out-talked him about the flowers. So he asks: why don't you change out of your female form? Some readers hear behind it an old view that certain attainments weren't open to a woman as a woman. To him, the question sounds reasonable. The goddess answers it twice. Once with words, and once with his own body. Today: Sariputra transformed.
screen: `PETALS STILL ON HIS ROBE.` → `WHY NOT CHANGE YOUR FORM?` → `SHE ANSWERS TWICE.`

segments.voice: First, the words, paraphrased. I've looked for the marks of being female, she says, and I haven't found them. So what would I change? Suppose a magician conjures up a woman. Would you ask the illusion to change her form? No, says Shariputra; an illusion has no fixed form to change. Just so, says the goddess. Nothing has a fixed form. Then, the second answer. By her power, she turns Shariputra into a likeness of herself, and herself into a likeness of Shariputra. And now the goddess, in Shariputra's form, asks Shariputra, in hers: why don't you change out of your female form? Shariputra answers, bewildered: I don't know how I turned into this. Then the goddess explains. If you could change out of it, then everyone in a woman's form could change. You aren't a woman, yet you appear as one. In the same way, all who appear as women aren't women in some fixed, final way. The Buddha taught that all things are neither male nor female. Then she lets him go back. Where is your female form now, she asks. Shariputra says: it isn't anywhere, and it isn't nowhere. And she says: that's how it is with all things. Afterward Vimalakirti tells Shariputra that this goddess has served many Buddhas and can take whatever birth she wishes. The Lotus, a few weeks ago, had the dragon king's daughter changing form to make a point. Here the question is turned around on the one asking it. The label he was sure of turns out not to be fixed.
screen: `I'VE LOOKED, AND FOUND NO MARKS.` · `A MAGICIAN'S ILLUSION.` · `I DON'T KNOW HOW I TURNED INTO THIS.` · `NEITHER MALE NOR FEMALE.` · then, large: `NOT FIXED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: question one fixed label. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind a label you wear, or one you've put on someone else. The shy one. The difficult one. Not a math person. Too old for that. Say it to yourself, then ask what the goddess asked: where exactly is it? Look for it the way she looked for the marks of being female. See if you can find where it begins and ends. You don't have to throw it away. Just notice whether it's as solid as it sounded. The bell holds the time.
Sariputra transformed. The goddess swaps forms with him to show that male and female aren't fixed, and asks why he doesn't change back. Today's word.
Your line: not fixed. Today, catch yourself once using a label on a person, and look for where it actually is. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read the goddess's exchange with Shariputra as a lesson on emptiness, that no form is fixed, and some modern Buddhist writers also draw on it in discussions of women in Buddhism.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra. the goddess has turned you into her likeness and asks why you don't change out of your female form. what do you say?

fork.reveal: he's bewildered, and the goddess answers: you aren't a woman, yet you appear as one; so it is with all who appear as women.

original.note: Sanskrit: emptiness, the teaching behind the goddess's answer that no form is fixed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick to win an argument.
what it means: the goddess swaps forms with Shariputra to show that male and female are appearances, not fixed natures.
what a scholar hears: the sutra applies emptiness to gender; some readers hear it answering a view that certain attainments were closed to women.

notes: Paraphrased from the Vimalakirti-nirdesha ch. 7, not quoted.
